A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that helps websites load faster. Normally, a website's files live on one machine called the origin server, which is the original computer storing the real, complete version of everything on that site. If every visitor worldwide had to fetch data from that single machine, loading would feel slow for anyone far away. A CDN solves this by copying popular files to many other computers, called edge locations, positioned closer to where people actually are. When someone requests a page, the network checks the nearest edge location first. If the needed file is already stored there, that's called a cache hit, and the page appears almost instantly since nothing had to travel far. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of the same popular book, so nobody has to travel to one distant central library every time. When a file isn't yet stored nearby, the edge location fetches it once from the origin server, then keeps a copy for the next request. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out traffic, and keeps sites running even during sudden surges in visitors.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer holding a website's real files | It's the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby computer storing copies of popular content | It lets pages load quickly for nearby visitors |
| Cache hit | When requested content is already stored nearby | It means near-instant loading, no long-distance trip |
| CDN | A network connecting origin servers to many edge locations | It keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
